record.original_question: Let a_1, ..., a_n be distinct decimal digits, with 1 <= n <= 9. Are there infinitely many prime numbers whose decimal expansion uses only those digits, possibly with repetition, while using no digits outside the chosen set?

evidence.quote: How many primes can we construct from all these digits only (eventually repeated) ?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let $1 \le n \le 9$ and let $S = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\} \subseteq \{0,1,2,\dots,9\}$ be a set of $n$ distinct decimal digits. Consider the set $P(S)$ of all prime numbers whose decimal expansion uses only digits from $S$ (each digit may be repeated, and no digit outside $S$ may appear). Excluding the trivially impossible cases (for instance $S \subseteq \{0\}$, or $S \subseteq \{0,2,4,5,6,8\}$ in which only finitely many primes can occur), determine whether $P(S)$ is infinite for every admissible choice of $S$. In particular, is it true that for any nonempty proper subset $S$ of $\{0,1,\dots,9\}$ that admits at least one prime, there exist infinitely many primes all of whose decimal digits lie in $S$?
artifact.status_search_result: The case in which exactly one decimal digit is forbidden (i.e. $n=9$) was settled by Maynard (Inventiones Math., 2019), who proved that there are infinitely many primes missing any prescribed decimal digit. Maynard's later work extends this to excluding $s$ digits in base $q$ when $q$ is large enough relative to $s$, but in base $10$ the methods are not strong enough to handle the case of two or more excluded digits. Thus for general $n \le 8$ (i.e. $\ge 2$ digits excluded), the problem is open.

status_evidence.title: Primes with restricted digits (Maynard, Invent. Math. 2019)
status_evidence.snippet: Maynard proves there are infinitely many primes with no digit equal to a prescribed digit a_0 in base 10.
status_evidence.claim: The case of excluding a single digit in base 10 is solved.

status_evidence.title: Primes and Polynomials With Restricted Digits (Maynard, IMRN 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: Asymptotic formulas for primes with s excluded digits hold provided q is large enough relative to s; the methods are not strong enough to give infinitely many primes with two missing digits in base 10.
status_evidence.claim: For base 10 with two or more excluded digits, the problem remains open.
